notes.definition: Metabolism is the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body. The energy transferred by respiration is used for the continual, enzyme-controlled reactions of metabolism that make new molecules.
explanation: Metabolism is the name for all the chemical reactions that happen in a cell or in the whole body. Some reactions build large molecules from small ones (synthesis), and some break large molecules down into small ones. Every one of these reactions is controlled by an enzyme, and they happen all the time.

Building new molecules needs energy. This energy is transferred by respiration, which is itself one of the reactions of metabolism. So respiration supplies the energy that allows cells to make the carbohydrates, lipids and proteins they need for growth, repair and storage.

Carbohydrates: glucose molecules are joined together to make larger carbohydrates. Plants convert glucose into starch (an energy store) and cellulose (which strengthens cell walls). Animals convert glucose into glycogen, which is their energy store, mainly in the liver and muscles. Lipids: one lipid molecule is made from one molecule of glycerol and three molecules of fatty acids.

Proteins: plants use glucose and nitrate ions to form amino acids. Amino acids are joined together to synthesise proteins, such as enzymes. Animals get their amino acids by digesting the proteins in their food and then build their own proteins from them. Excess proteins (amino acids) cannot be stored, so they are broken down to form urea, which is excreted in urine.

This shows why small molecules are so important. Sugars (such as glucose), amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol are the building blocks: they are joined together to synthesise carbohydrates, proteins and lipids, and they are the products released when those large molecules are broken down, for example during digestion. They can then be rebuilt into new large molecules or used in respiration.
keyFacts: Metabolism is the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body.
Metabolic reactions are controlled by enzymes and happen continually.
Energy transferred by respiration is used to synthesise new molecules.
Glucose is converted to starch and cellulose in plants, and to glycogen in animals.
A lipid molecule is made from one glycerol molecule and three fatty acid molecules.
Glucose and nitrate ions are used to form amino acids, which are used to synthesise proteins.
Excess proteins are broken down to form urea for excretion.
Sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol are the building blocks of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids.

keyTerms.definition: The sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body.
A storage carbohydrate made from glucose in animals, mainly in the liver and muscles.
A fat or oil; one molecule is made from one glycerol molecule and three fatty acid molecules.
A waste product formed from the breakdown of excess proteins (amino acids); it is excreted in urine.
Building larger molecules from smaller ones; these reactions need energy from respiration.
A protein that acts as a biological catalyst, controlling the rate of a metabolic reaction.

workedExamples.title: Classifying metabolic reactions
workedExamples.question: Sort these reactions into 'synthesis' or 'breakdown': (a) glucose → glycogen, (b) excess proteins → urea, (c) amino acids → protein, (d) glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
steps: Synthesis means small molecules are joined to make larger ones.
(a) Many glucose molecules join to form glycogen: synthesis.
(b) Proteins are broken down to make urea: breakdown.
(c) Amino acids join to make a protein: synthesis.
(d) Respiration breaks glucose down into smaller molecules: breakdown.

workedExamples.title: Building blocks of large molecules
workedExamples.question: Name the smaller molecules used to make (a) glycogen, (b) a lipid and (c) a protein.
steps: (a) Glycogen is a carbohydrate made from glucose (a sugar).
(b) A lipid is made from one glycerol and three fatty acids.
(c) A protein is made from amino acids joined together.
workedExamples.answer: (a) glucose; (b) glycerol and three fatty acids; (c) amino acids

workedExamples.title: Following an amino acid
workedExamples.question: A person eats more protein than their body needs. Describe what happens to the extra protein.
steps: Proteins in food are digested into amino acids, which are absorbed into the blood.
Some amino acids are used to synthesise the body's own proteins.
Excess amino acids cannot be stored, so they are broken down to form urea.
workedExamples.answer: It is digested to amino acids; the excess is broken down to urea, which is excreted.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think metabolism just means how fast you burn food or digest.
misconceptions.right: In fact metabolism is the sum of ALL the reactions in a cell or the body, including building molecules (synthesis), respiration and breaking down excess proteins.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think animals store glucose as starch.
misconceptions.right: In fact animals store glucose as glycogen. Starch is the storage carbohydrate in plants.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a lipid is made from three glycerol molecules and one fatty acid.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is the other way round: one glycerol molecule and three fatty acid molecules.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think excess protein is stored in the body for later.
misconceptions.right: In fact excess proteins (amino acids) cannot be stored; they are broken down to form urea, which is excreted.

realWorld: Athletes eat carbohydrate-rich meals before endurance events to increase the glycogen stored in their muscles and liver.
Doctors measure urea in the blood to check how well the kidneys are removing waste, because urea comes from the breakdown of excess proteins.
Cotton fibres are almost pure cellulose, and wood is mainly cellulose: both come from plant metabolism converting glucose into cell wall material.
examTips: Learn the definition exactly: 'the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body'.
For lipids, always give the numbers: ONE glycerol and THREE fatty acids.
Match each storage carbohydrate to the right organism: starch and cellulose in plants, glycogen in animals.
When a question asks about 'importance' of small molecules, explain both roles: building larger molecules (synthesis) and being released when those molecules are broken down.
Remember that respiration is itself part of metabolism, and it provides the energy for synthesis reactions.
summary: Metabolism is the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body.
Metabolic reactions are enzyme-controlled and use energy from respiration to make new molecules.
Glucose + nitrate ions → amino acids → proteins.
Excess proteins are broken down to urea for excretion.
Sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol are the building blocks of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids.

questions.question: What is metabolism?
options: The digestion of food in the stomach
The sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body
The rate at which the heart beats
The removal of waste from the body
markScheme: 1 mark: the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body
questions.explanation: Metabolism covers every reaction: synthesis, respiration and breakdown. Digestion and excretion involve some metabolic reactions, but they are not the whole of metabolism.

questions.question: Which molecules are joined together to make one lipid molecule?
options: Three glycerol molecules and one fatty acid
One glycerol molecule and three fatty acids
markScheme: 1 mark: one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids
questions.explanation: A lipid is formed from one glycerol and three fatty acids. Swapping the numbers is a common mistake. Glucose makes carbohydrates, and amino acids make proteins.

markScheme: 1 mark: amino acids
questions.explanation: Amino acids are joined in chains to make proteins. Fatty acids and glycerol make lipids, and glucose makes carbohydrates.

questions.question: Excess proteins in the body are broken down to form which substance for excretion?
markScheme: 1 mark: urea
questions.explanation: Excess proteins cannot be stored, so they are broken down to form urea, which is excreted in urine. Glycogen and starch are carbohydrate stores, and lactic acid comes from anaerobic respiration.

questions.question: Which conversion is part of metabolism in animals but NOT in plants?
markScheme: 1 mark: glucose → glycogen
questions.explanation: Animals store glucose as glycogen. Plants store it as starch and make cellulose for cell walls. Only plants make amino acids from glucose and nitrate ions; animals get amino acids from their food.

questions.question: What controls the reactions of metabolism?
markScheme: 1 mark: enzymes
questions.explanation: Every metabolic reaction is catalysed by an enzyme. Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration happens, but they do not control all reactions. Urea is a waste product.

questions.question: Which of these metabolic reactions is a breakdown reaction rather than a synthesis reaction?
markScheme: 1 mark: excess proteins → urea
questions.explanation: Forming urea from excess proteins breaks large molecules down. The other three join small molecules together to make larger ones, which is synthesis.

questions.question: Where does the energy used in metabolism to synthesise new molecules come from?
markScheme: 1 mark: respiration
questions.explanation: Respiration transfers energy that cells use for enzyme-controlled synthesis reactions. Animal cells do not photosynthesise, and urea is a waste product, not an energy source.

questions.question: Plants use glucose and which other substance to make amino acids?
markScheme: 1 mark: nitrate ions
questions.explanation: Amino acids contain nitrogen, which plants take in as nitrate ions from the soil. Fatty acids and glycerol are used to make lipids.

questions.question: Which substance is made from glucose by plant cells but NOT by animal cells?
markScheme: 1 mark: cellulose
questions.explanation: Only plant cells have cellulose cell walls. Glycogen is made by animals, not plants. Both plants and animals make lipids and proteins.

questions.question: Why do mammals convert excess proteins into urea?
options: Urea is used to make glycogen
Urea is a source of energy for the muscles
Excess proteins cannot be stored, and urea can be excreted
Urea is needed to make new amino acids
markScheme: 1 mark: excess proteins cannot be stored, and urea can be excreted
questions.explanation: The body has no store for excess amino acids, so they are broken down and the nitrogen-containing part is turned into urea, which is removed in urine. Urea is waste, not a fuel or building block.

questions.question: A muscle cell is growing and making many new proteins. Which does it need more of?
options: Amino acids, and energy transferred by respiration
markScheme: 1 mark: amino acids, and energy transferred by respiration
questions.explanation: Proteins are built from amino acids, and synthesis reactions need energy, which comes from respiration. Fatty acids and glycerol make lipids, not proteins, and urea is waste.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a metabolic reaction?
options: Synthesis of proteins from amino acids
Breakdown of excess proteins to form urea
Diffusion of oxygen into the blood
markScheme: 1 mark: diffusion of oxygen into the blood
questions.explanation: Diffusion is the movement of particles, not a chemical reaction, so it is not part of metabolism. The other three are chemical reactions controlled by enzymes.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows parts of three carbohydrate molecules.
What do starch, glycogen and cellulose have in common?
options: They are all made from glucose molecules joined together
They are all made from amino acids
They are all made from glycerol and fatty acids
They are all broken down to form urea
markScheme: 1 mark: they are all made from glucose molecules joined together
questions.explanation: All three are carbohydrates built from glucose. Amino acids make proteins, glycerol and fatty acids make lipids, and urea comes from excess proteins.

questions.question: Define the term metabolism.
acceptedAnswers: all the reactions in a cell or the body
markScheme: 1 mark: the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body
questions.explanation: The key word is 'all'. Metabolism is not just digestion or respiration but every reaction in a cell or the body.

markScheme: 1 mark: urea
questions.explanation: Urea is made from excess proteins (amino acids) and excreted in urine. Do not confuse it with urine itself or with uric acid.

questions.question: Explain why respiration is important for the other reactions of metabolism.
markScheme: 1 mark: respiration transfers energy
1 mark: which is used for (enzyme-controlled) reactions that synthesise new / larger molecules
questions.explanation: Synthesis reactions such as making proteins or glycogen need energy. Respiration supplies that energy, and it is a metabolic reaction itself.

questions.question:
Glucose is used to make three different carbohydrates.
Name the three carbohydrates and give the type of organism (plant or animal) that makes each one.
markScheme: 1 mark: starch, made by plants
1 mark: cellulose, made by plants
1 mark: glycogen, made by animals
questions.explanation: Starch and glycogen are energy stores in plants and animals respectively. Cellulose strengthens plant cell walls.

questions.question: Describe how plants make proteins.
markScheme: 1 mark: glucose and nitrate ions are used to form amino acids
1 mark: amino acids are joined together to synthesise proteins
questions.explanation: Nitrate ions provide the nitrogen that glucose lacks. The amino acids are the building blocks; proteins are long chains of them.

questions.question: Explain why amino acids are important in both the synthesis and the breakdown of proteins in the human body.
acceptedAnswers: excess amino acids broken down to urea
markScheme: 1 mark: proteins are synthesised by joining amino acids together
1 mark: when proteins are broken down (e.g. digested), amino acids are released / can be reused to build new proteins
1 mark: excess amino acids are broken down to form urea, which is excreted
questions.explanation: Amino acids are both the building blocks and the breakdown products of proteins. Food proteins are digested to amino acids, rebuilt into human proteins, and any excess ends up as urea.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the mass of urea in a person's urine over one day on a normal diet and over one day on a very high-protein diet.
Suggest why the mass of urea is higher on the high-protein diet.

headers: Mass of urea in urine in g per day

markScheme: 1 mark: more protein / amino acids than the body needs, and these cannot be stored
1 mark: so the excess is broken down to form urea, which is excreted in urine
questions.explanation: The body only uses as many amino acids as it needs for protein synthesis. The rest are broken down, producing more urea for excretion.

questions.question: Metabolism includes reactions that build up molecules and reactions that break them down. Give one example of each.
acceptedAnswers: lipid from glycerol and fatty acids
markScheme: 1 mark: build-up example, e.g. glucose → starch / glycogen / cellulose; glycerol + fatty acids → lipid; amino acids → proteins
1 mark: breakdown example, e.g. respiration; excess proteins → urea
questions.explanation: Building up (synthesis) joins small molecules together; breaking down splits large molecules into smaller ones.

questions.question: Explain why fatty acids and glycerol are important in the metabolism of lipids.
acceptedAnswers: lipids made from glycerol and fatty acids
lipids broken down into fatty acids and glycerol
markScheme: 1 mark: lipids are synthesised from one glycerol and three fatty acids
1 mark: when lipids are broken down (e.g. in digestion), fatty acids and glycerol are released and can be used to build new lipids (or used for energy)
questions.explanation: Fatty acids and glycerol are the building blocks of lipids. Breaking a lipid down releases them, and they can be reassembled into the body's own lipids.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows some properties of glucose and starch.
Suggest why plants convert glucose into starch for storage, rather than storing glucose itself.
markScheme: 1 mark: starch / glycogen are large, insoluble molecules
1 mark: so they do not affect the movement of water by osmosis / do not move out of the cells
questions.explanation: Lots of dissolved glucose would cause water to move into cells by osmosis. Large insoluble storage molecules avoid this and can be broken back down to glucose when needed.

questions.question: Describe examples of reactions that are part of metabolism. Include reactions that build molecules and reactions that break molecules down.
markScheme: Indicative content: metabolism is the sum of all reactions in a cell or body; reactions are enzyme-controlled; synthesis examples: glucose → starch and cellulose in plants, glucose → glycogen in animals; one glycerol + three fatty acids → lipid; glucose + nitrate ions → amino acids (plants); amino acids → proteins; breakdown examples: respiration (glucose → carbon dioxide + water, transferring energy); breakdown of excess proteins → urea for excretion; energy from respiration is used for synthesis.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes several correct examples of both synthesis and breakdown with detail, such as the building blocks or the organism involved.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): gives one or two examples, or only one type of reaction.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Cover both sides of metabolism. Naming the building blocks (glucose, glycerol and fatty acids, amino acids) and the products shows a secure understanding.

questions.question: Explain the importance of sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol in the synthesis and breakdown of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids.
markScheme: Indicative content: sugars (glucose) are joined to make carbohydrates: starch and cellulose in plants, glycogen in animals; carbohydrates are broken down to sugars (e.g. starch digested to sugars, glycogen and starch converted back to glucose) which can be used in respiration; amino acids are joined to synthesise proteins (e.g. enzymes); plants make amino acids from glucose and nitrate ions; proteins are broken down (digested) to amino acids, which can be rebuilt into new proteins; excess amino acids/proteins are broken down to urea and excreted; one glycerol and three fatty acids form a lipid; lipids are broken down to fatty acids and glycerol; synthesis reactions are enzyme-controlled and need energy from respiration; so these small molecules are the building blocks and also the breakdown products, allowing materials to be stored, transported and reused.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed and coherent explanation covering all three groups of large molecules, describing both synthesis and breakdown, with correct building blocks and links to energy from respiration or urea.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains synthesis and/or breakdown for at least two groups of molecules with mostly correct building blocks.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements linking one or more small molecules to the large molecule they make.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Organise the answer by molecule type: carbohydrates (sugars), proteins (amino acids), lipids (glycerol and fatty acids). For each, describe how it is built and what it breaks down into. Mentioning energy from respiration and the fate of excess amino acids lifts the answer to Level 3.
